usamo-usamo-2011-02.title: An invariant mod 5 and the lattice of moves
usamo-usamo-2011-02.body:
Label the vertices $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ around the pentagon (indices mod $5$) and let $N_j$ be the number at vertex $j$. The edge opposite vertex $i$ is $\{i+2, i+3\}$, so a turn at vertex $i$ with amount $m$ adds $m L_i$ to the vector $N = (N_0, \dots, N_4)$, where
$$L_i = 2e_i - e_{i+2} - e_{i+3}$$
and $e_j$ are the standard basis vectors. Turns commute and $m$ may be any integer, so the reachable vectors are exactly $N + \Lambda$, where $\Lambda$ is the set of integer combinations of $L_0, \dots, L_4$.

**At most one vertex.** Let $S(N) = \sum_j jN_j \bmod 5$. A turn at $i$ changes $S$ by $m\,(2i - (i+2) - (i+3)) = -5m \equiv 0$, so $S$ is invariant. A win at vertex $v$ has $S = 2011v \equiv v \pmod 5$. So the game can only be won at the vertex $v \equiv S(N)$.

**The game can be won at that vertex.** We prove: *if $y \in \mathbb Z^5$ satisfies $\sum_j y_j = 0$ and $\sum_j jy_j \equiv 0 \pmod 5$, then $y \in \Lambda$.*

Put $g_k = e_k - e_{k+2}$. Then
$$L_i = (e_i - e_{i+2}) - (e_{i+3} - e_{i+5}) = g_i - g_{i+3},$$
so $g_i \equiv g_{i+3} \pmod\Lambda$. Adding $3$ repeatedly runs through all residues mod $5$, so all $g_k$ are congruent mod $\Lambda$ to $g := g_0$. Also $\sum_k g_k = 0$, so $5g \in \Lambda$.

Telescoping, $e_0 - e_{2t} = g_0 + g_2 + \dots + g_{2t-2} \equiv t\,g \pmod\Lambda$ for $t \ge 0$. For a vertex $j$ take $t_j \in \{0,\dots,4\}$ with $2t_j \equiv j$, i.e. $t_j \equiv 3j \pmod 5$; then $e_j \equiv e_0 - t_j g$. Hence for $y$ as above,
$$y = \sum_j y_je_j \equiv \Big(\sum_j y_j\Big)e_0 - \Big(\sum_j t_jy_j\Big) g = -\Big(\sum_j t_jy_j\Big) g \pmod\Lambda.$$
Now $\sum_j t_j y_j \equiv 3\sum_j jy_j \equiv 0 \pmod 5$, so the right side is an integer multiple of $5g \in \Lambda$. Thus $y \in \Lambda$.

Apply this to $y = 2011e_v - N$ with $v \equiv S(N)$: $\sum_j y_j = 2011 - 2011 = 0$ and $\sum_j jy_j \equiv 2011v - S(N) \equiv v - S(N) \equiv 0 \pmod 5$. So $2011e_v = N + y$ is reachable: writing $y = \sum c_iL_i$, perform a turn at each vertex $i$ with $m = c_i$.

Hence for every starting position the game can be won at exactly one vertex. ∎

usamo-usamo-2011-03.title: Uniqueness up to similarity plus a model hexagon
usamo-usamo-2011-03.body:
Call a simple hexagon *satisfying* if its angles obey $\angle A = 3\angle D$, $\angle C = 3\angle F$, $\angle E = 3\angle B$, it has $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $CD = FA$, and no two opposite sides are parallel. Put $\beta = \angle B$, $\delta = \angle D$, $\varphi = \angle F$. The angle sum of a hexagon is $720^\circ$, so $4(\beta + \delta + \varphi) = 720^\circ$, i.e. $\beta + \delta + \varphi = 180^\circ$. Also each interior angle is below $360^\circ$, so $\beta, \delta, \varphi < 120^\circ$.

**Step 1: directions of the sides.** Traverse the hexagon counterclockwise (reflect it if necessary) and let $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_6$ be the directions of the side vectors $\vec{AB}, \vec{BC}, \vec{CD}, \vec{DE}, \vec{EF}, \vec{FA}$. At a vertex with interior angle $V$ the direction turns by $180^\circ - V$. Taking $\theta_1 = 0$ and using $\beta + \delta + \varphi = 180^\circ$ (all mod $360^\circ$):
$$\theta_2 = 180^\circ - \beta,\quad \theta_3 = -\beta - 3\varphi,\quad \theta_4 = -2\varphi,\quad \theta_5 = 180^\circ - 3\beta - 2\varphi,\quad \theta_6 = -3\beta - 3\varphi.$$
So opposite sides $AB, DE$ are parallel iff $2\varphi \equiv 0 \pmod{180^\circ}$, i.e. $\varphi = 90^\circ$; similarly $BC \parallel EF$ iff $\delta = 90^\circ$ and $CD \parallel FA$ iff $\beta = 90^\circ$. Hence in a satisfying hexagon $\beta, \delta, \varphi \ne 90^\circ$.

**Step 2: a satisfying hexagon is determined by its angles up to similarity.** Let $d_k$ be the unit vector of direction $\theta_k$ and $p = AB = DE$, $q = BC = EF$, $r = CD = FA$. Closing up the hexagon gives
$$p\,\vec x + q\,\vec y + r\,\vec z = \vec 0, \qquad \vec x = d_1 + d_4,\ \vec y = d_2 + d_5,\ \vec z = d_3 + d_6.$$
Since $d_1 + d_4 = 2\cos\frac{\theta_1-\theta_4}{2}\,\big(\text{unit vector at angle } \tfrac{\theta_1+\theta_4}2\big)$, the vector $\vec x$ is nonzero (as $AB \nparallel DE$) with direction $\frac{\theta_1+\theta_4}{2} = -\varphi \pmod{180^\circ}$; likewise $\vec y \ne 0$ has direction $\frac{\theta_2+\theta_5}{2} \equiv -2\beta - \varphi$. These differ by $2\beta \not\equiv 0 \pmod{180^\circ}$ since $\beta \ne 90^\circ$, so $\vec x, \vec y$ are linearly independent. Then for given $r$ the equation $p\vec x + q\vec y = -r\vec z$ has a unique solution $(p, q)$, so the ratio $p : q : r$ is determined by the angles. The angles give all side directions (up to a common rotation) and the ratios give all side lengths (up to a common factor), so **any two satisfying hexagons with the same $\beta, \delta, \varphi$ are similar** (with vertices corresponding in order).

**Step 3: a model hexagon.** Take a triangle $A'C'E'$ with $\angle A' = \delta$, $\angle C' = \varphi$, $\angle E' = \beta$ (possible since the angles are positive with sum $180^\circ$), and let $B'$, $D'$, $F'$ be the reflections of $E'$, $A'$, $C'$ across lines $A'C'$, $C'E'$, $E'A'$ respectively. The three reflected triangles $A'B'C'$, $C'D'E'$, $E'F'A'$ lie outside $A'C'E'$; at vertex $C'$ the triangle and the two flaps occupy angles $\varphi, \varphi, \varphi$, and $3\varphi < 360^\circ$, so the flaps meeting at $C'$ do not overlap (same at $A'$, $E'$). So $A'B'C'D'E'F'$ is a simple hexagon with
$$\angle B' = \angle A'E'C' = \beta,\quad \angle D' = \delta,\quad \angle F' = \varphi,\quad \angle A' = 3\delta,\quad \angle C' = 3\varphi,\quad \angle E' = 3\beta,$$
and reflection gives $A'B' = A'E' = D'E'$, $B'C' = E'C' = E'F'$, $C'D' = C'A' = F'A'$. Its opposite sides are not parallel by Step 1 (the angles are the same as for $ABCDEF$). So it is satisfying.

Moreover $D'$ is the reflection of $A'$ across $C'E'$, so line $A'D'$ is perpendicular to $C'E'$ through $A'$: it is the altitude from $A'$ of triangle $A'C'E'$. Likewise $C'F'$ and $E'B'$ are the other two altitudes. The altitudes of a triangle concur (at its orthocenter), so $A'D'$, $B'E'$, $C'F'$ are concurrent.

**Conclusion.** By Step 2, $ABCDEF$ is similar to $A'B'C'D'E'F'$ with corresponding vertices, and a similarity maps concurrent lines to concurrent lines. Therefore $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ are concurrent. ∎

usamo-usamo-2011-05.title: Isogonal conjugates from the intersection point
usamo-usamo-2011-05.body:
If $AB \parallel CD$, the two conditions are the same statement. So assume lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at a point $X$. We show that then line $Q_1Q_2$ passes through $X$ (when $Q_1 \ne Q_2$); since $Q_1$ lies inside $ABCD$, it is not on line $AB$ or $CD$, so line $Q_1Q_2$ — a line through $X$ different from $AB$ and $CD$ — is parallel to neither. Thus both conditions are false and the equivalence holds.

Relabelling $(A, B, C, D) \to (B, A, D, C)$ describes the same quadrilateral and swaps the definitions of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, so we may assume $X$ lies beyond $A$ and $D$, i.e. $A$ is between $X$ and $B$ and $D$ is between $X$ and $C$.

**Isogonal conjugates.** Recall: for a triangle and a point $Z$ not on its side lines, reflect each line joining a vertex to $Z$ across the angle bisector at that vertex; the three reflected lines concur at the *isogonal conjugate* of $Z$. (Reflecting across the internal or the external bisector gives the same line.)

*Triangle $XBC$.* Its angle at $B$ is $\angle ABC$ and at $C$ is $\angle BCD$. Since $\angle Q_1BC = \angle ABP$ and both rays $BQ_1$, $BP$ lie inside this angle, line $BQ_1$ is the reflection of line $BP$ across the bisector at $B$; similarly line $CQ_1$ is the reflection of $CP$ at $C$. These two lines meet only at $Q_1$, so $Q_1$ is the isogonal conjugate of $P$ in triangle $XBC$. Hence $Q_1$ lies on the reflection $\ell$ of line $XP$ across the bisector of the angle between lines $XB$ and $XC$.

*Triangle $XAD$.* $P$ is not on its side lines ($P$ is interior to $ABCD$). From $\angle Q_2AD = \angle BAP$, line $AQ_2$ is the reflection of line $AP$ across the bisector of angle $BAD$; that is a bisector of the pair of lines $AX\,(= AB)$ and $AD$. Likewise $DQ_2$ is the reflection of $DP$ for the lines $DX\,(= DC)$ and $DA$. So $Q_2$ is the isogonal conjugate of $P$ in triangle $XAD$, and $Q_2$ lies on the reflection of line $XP$ across a bisector of the lines $XA, XD$ — which are the same lines $XB, XC$ as before. So $Q_2 \in \ell$ too.

Therefore $X, Q_1, Q_2$ all lie on $\ell$, and as explained above, $Q_1Q_2$ is then parallel to neither $AB$ nor $CD$. In all cases, $Q_1Q_2 \parallel AB \iff Q_1Q_2 \parallel CD$. ∎

usamo-usamo-2011-06.title: Double counting and Cauchy–Schwarz
usamo-usamo-2011-06.body:
Let $U = A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{11}$ with $|U| = N$, and for $u \in U$ let $x_u$ be the number of indices $i$ with $u \in A_i$ (so $x_u \ge 1$).

**Two counts.** Counting pairs (element, set containing it):
$$\sum_{u \in U} x_u = \sum_{i=1}^{11}|A_i| = 11 \cdot 45 = 495.$$
Counting triples (element, two different sets containing it):
$$\sum_{u\in U}\binom{x_u}{2} = \sum_{i<j}|A_i \cap A_j| = \binom{11}{2}\cdot 9 = 495.$$
Hence $\sum x_u^2 = 2\cdot 495 + \sum x_u = 1485$.

**Cauchy–Schwarz.** $\left(\sum_u x_u\right)^2 \le N \sum_u x_u^2$, so
$$N \ge \frac{495^2}{1485} = \frac{245025}{1485} = 165.$$

**Equality.** Let $U$ be the set of all $\binom{11}{3} = 165$ three-element subsets of $\{1, \dots, 11\}$, and add $60$ further elements to get a set $A$ of size $225$. Let $A_i$ be the set of triples containing $i$. Then $|A_i| = \binom{10}{2} = 45$, $|A_i \cap A_j| = \binom 91 = 9$ (triples containing both $i$ and $j$), and $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{11} = U$ has exactly $165$ elements. ∎
